title: The Tongue-Cut Sparrow

provenance.rights: The text is our own retelling of a traditional Japanese folk tale, written for Omramo; it does not use the wording of the cited edition. The cited edition is in the US public domain (published before 1931); other territories not verified. Legal review pending (PRD Q23).

geography.lesson: Japan is a country of islands, with wooded hills and bamboo groves where sparrows gather.

culture.lesson: Rice is the daily food of Japan. A guest is welcomed with bows, tea and the best seat, and a polite guest takes the smaller gift.

moral.lesson: Kindness is returned. Greed chooses the big basket and regrets it.
moral.reflectionQuestion: Which basket would you have picked, and why?

moral: Kindness comes back to you, but greed brings only trouble.

card.title: The Old Man
card.body: He cuts wood in the hills and shares his supper with a sparrow. When his friend is lost, he walks all day to find her.

card.label: Character · in Part I and Part II
card.title: The Sparrow
card.body: She is small and brown, and she bows to everyone. She forgives quickly, and she never forgets a friend.

paras: ^An old man and his wife lived below the green hills.
Their house had a thick straw roof. Behind it a <tap:bamboo-grove>bamboo grove</tap> whispered in the wind.
The <name:old-man>old man</name> had a small friend, a brown <name:sparrow>Sparrow</name>. Every morning she hopped along the porch to meet him.
<say:sparrow*>“Chun, chun!”</say> she sang. <say:sparrow>“Good morning!”</say>
Every evening the old man came home from the hills with firewood on his back.
He sat down with his bowl of <tap:rice>rice</tap>. He took one bite. Then he put a few grains in his hand.
<say:old-man*>“One for me,”</say> he said, <say:old-man>“and one for you, little friend.”</say>
The Sparrow ate from his hand, grain by grain by grain.
One day the old man went up the hill to cut wood. It was washing day.
His wife, the <name:old-woman>old woman</name>, had a heap of clothes to wash. Her back ached. Her hands were sore.
She had cooked a bowl of rice paste to make the clothes smooth and stiff. But when she reached for it, the bowl was empty.
Down hopped the Sparrow and bowed her little head.
<say:sparrow*>“I ate it,”</say> she said. <say:sparrow>“I thought it was my breakfast. I am sorry.”</say>
But the old woman was too tired and too cross to listen. <pop:1.3>Snip!</pop> went her scissors, and nipped the tip of the Sparrow’s tongue.
<say:old-woman*>“Shoo!”</say> she cried. <say:old-woman>“Be off!”</say> And the Sparrow flew away over the bamboo.
That evening the porch was quiet. No hop, no song, no small brown friend.
<say:old-man*>“Where is my Sparrow?”</say> asked the old man.
<say:old-woman*>“She ate my paste, so I chased her away,”</say> said the old woman, banging the pots.
The old man could not eat his rice. At first light he tied on his sandals and went to find her.
The bamboo stood tall and green on every side. A clear, cold stream ran over the stones.
A <tap:himeji-moment>white heron</tap> stood in the water, as still as a post.
<say:old-man*>“Sparrow, Sparrow, where is your home?”</say> called the old man.
The heron only blinked. The bamboo only creaked.
He walked on, up the hill and down the hill. <say:old-man*>“Sparrow, Sparrow, where is your home?”</say>
The sun climbed high. His legs grew tired. <say:old-man*>“Sparrow, Sparrow, where is your home?”</say>
<say:sparrow*>“Chun, chun! Here I am!”</say>
There on a little gate sat the Sparrow. <say:sparrow*>“My tongue is quite well again,”</say> she said. <say:sparrow>“Come in, dear friend!”</say>
Behind the gate stood a small house of pale wood.
All the Sparrow’s family came and bowed. The old man bowed back.
<say:sparrow*>“You are our <tap:guest>guest</tap>,”</say> said the Sparrow. <say:sparrow>“Sit here, in the best place.”</say>
They brought him hot tea and rice cakes and sweet red beans. Then the young sparrows danced, flip, flap, flutter, and the old man laughed.
^When the sun dipped low, it was time to go home.
The sparrows carried in two baskets. One was big and heavy. One was small and light.
<say:sparrow*>“A gift for you,”</say> said the Sparrow. <say:sparrow>“Please choose.”</say>
<say:old-man*>“I am old,”</say> said the old man, <say:old-man>“and the small one is enough. Thank you, little friend.”</say>
At home the old man lifted the lid of the small basket.
Out shone gold coins, rolls of silk, and coral as red as berries.
<say:old-woman*>“There was a big one too?”</say> cried the old woman. <say:old-woman>“And you left it behind? I shall fetch it myself!”</say>
<say:old-man*>“We have enough,”</say> said the old man. But she was already tying on her sandals.
The old woman marched through the bamboo. Stamp, stamp, stamp.
She did not bow. She did not say good day. She did not say sorry.
<say:old-woman*>“No tea for me,”</say> she said. <say:old-woman>“I have come for the big basket.”</say>
<say:sparrow*>“Then please take it,”</say> said the Sparrow, and she bowed as politely as ever.
The big basket was heavy. It bumped on her back all along the hill road.
<say:old-woman*>“Gold,”</say> she puffed. <say:old-woman>“Silk. Coral. Heaps and heaps of it!”</say>
The evening sky turned pale and pink. Home was still far away, and she could not wait one step more.
She sat down on the road and pulled off the lid.
<pop:1.3>Buzz!</pop> Out flew a cloud of bees.
<pop:1.3>Plop!</pop> Out hopped a fat brown toad, and sat on her foot.
Under the toad there was only mud and stones. Not one coin. Not one thread of silk.
<say:old-woman*>“Oh, oh, oh!”</say> cried the old woman. She ran all the way home, with the bees humming behind her.
The old woman tumbled in with mud on her nose.
<say:old-woman*>“I was cross and greedy,”</say> she puffed, <say:old-woman>“and I am sorry. The small basket was enough.”</say>
After that, she put out rice each morning for every sparrow in the hills. The old man’s friend always came first.
And on washing days, she made two bowls of paste. Just in case.

landmarks.name: Himeji Castle

built.note: The castle as it stands today. Older forts stood on the same hill before it; their dates are to verify (CONTENT_PLAN §5).

low.line: A tall white castle on a hill. Its roofs curve up like a bird's wings.

medium.line: A white castle in Himeji, Japan, finished about 400 years ago.
medium.note: People call it the White Heron Castle, for its white walls and wing-like roofs.

advanced.line: A hilltop castle built between 1601 and 1609, called the White Heron Castle for its white walls and wing-like roofs.
advanced.note: Its wooden towers are coated in white plaster. Most castles of its age in Japan have been lost; this one still stands.

art.alt: A white castle with many curved grey roofs, one above another, on a stone base on a green hill.

sourceNotes: This is our own retelling, written for Omramo, of a traditional Japanese folk tale,
Shita-kiri Suzume (The Tongue-Cut Sparrow). It is not the wording of any earlier edition.
Documented source for the tale: Yei Theodora Ozaki, "Japanese Fairy Tales" (1908 edition),
(US public domain; other territories not verified).
Softened for ability age 6 to 8: the scissors only nip the tip of the Sparrow's tongue and she is soon well;
the old woman is tired and hasty on washing day, not wicked; the big basket holds bees, a toad, mud and
stones in place of the demons and snake of the source; she says sorry and changes her ways.
Left out: the old woman showing the cut tongue, the scolding speeches, and the sparrows' wish to punish her.
Status: DRAFT. Text review pending. Cultural review (standard: Japanese reader) pending.

palette.mood: Fresh bamboo greens and pale washed sky, warm straw and wood, one small note of vermilion; gentle and airy like a brush painting.

artBrief.light: Soft morning to early evening; one warm light from the upper left in every picture. The road scene is early evening with a pale pink sky, never night.
world: Old rural Japan before 1600: a small farmhouse (minka) with a thick, steep thatched roof, wooden posts, earth walls, sliding wooden doors and a narrow raised wooden porch (engawa). Woven straw mats on the floor inside.
Low wooded hills behind the house: cedar and pine on the slopes, bamboo at the foot. Draw slim native bamboo (madake) with clear rings and feathery leaves, not giant thick canes.

Clothes: plain indigo-blue or undyed cotton or hemp work clothes, a short jacket tied with a cloth belt, leggings, straw sandals (waraji). The old woman wears a plain cloth tied over her hair. No bright silk kimono, no fans, no formal hairpins.

Tools: firewood tied in a bundle on a wooden back frame; a round wooden washtub; washed cloth stretched flat on long boards to dry in the sun; a glazed bowl for the rice paste; small U-shaped spring scissors made of one piece of iron (nigiri-basami), not modern crossed scissors.
The sparrow is the Eurasian tree sparrow, the common sparrow of Japan: chestnut-brown cap, white cheeks with a black spot, black bib, streaked brown back. Keep the sparrows as birds; no clothes.
The white heron is a white egret: all white, slim neck, dark legs, standing in shallow water. It is only a bird in the stream. Himeji Castle never appears in any scene.
The two baskets are lidded wicker boxes (tsuzura) with carrying cords, one very big and one small. Treasure: small plain oval gold pieces, rolls of coloured silk, a branch of red coral.
Food at the sparrows' house: small cups of green tea, round white rice cakes, sweet red beans, on low trays.
The nuisance from the big basket is funny, not scary: round bumbling bees, one fat friendly toad, mud and stones. No stinging, no monsters, no snake.

Avoid: Mount Fuji, cherry blossom, torii gates, pagodas, samurai, geisha, lanterns everywhere, and any castle in the scenes. Avoid slanted-eye caricature; draw the old couple as warm, particular people.

characters.old-man: Small, thin and a little bent, with a round kind face, white topknot and wispy white eyebrows. Faded indigo-blue cotton jacket and leggings, straw sandals. Signature details: the bundle of firewood on his back, and an open hand with rice grains.
characters.sparrow: A plump little tree sparrow: chestnut cap, white cheeks with a black spot, bright black eye. Signature gesture: a polite bow with wings a little open.
characters.old-woman: Short and sturdy, sleeves tied back for work, a plain plum-coloured cloth over grey hair. Tired eyes and a cross mouth in Part I and most of Part II; a soft, sorry smile on the last page. Never ugly or witch-like.
